---
name: project-gl-budget-and-gl-ports
description: "GL budget harness (tools/gl_budget.py) and the Morph3D and CubicGrid ports, all merged 2026-10-09/10; accuracy about 10 percent; follow-up issue #50 and an overnight capture pending"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
---

Merged to `main`: `tools/gl_budget.py` (host harness, instrumented private TinyGL copy, cost model fitted to Gears), Morph3D (PR #48) and CubicGrid (PR #49, registered with `*ticks: 20`). Issues #41 and #45 are closed. Accuracy against the board is about 10 percent on four scenes not used in the fit (table in `docs/gl-budget.md`); Gears' "measured" rows come from #43, not a fresh capture.

**Open follow-up: #50.** Morph3D picks one of four shapes at random and the device does not seed `random()`; the two middle shapes (5,040 and 5,100 vertices, predicted step about 66 to 68 ms) have never appeared. CubicGrid has had only a 45 s capture. Plan agreed with Rod on 2026-10-10: flash `-DROTATE_SECONDS=10` (default badge) and capture two hours or more while he sleeps, then add results to `docs/gl-budget.md` and `tools/assessment_measured.md` on a branch (not `main` without asking). Leave the board rotating and ask before flashing the normal build back.

**Why:** Rod wants Gears, Morph3D and CubicGrid on the board to judge the harness before using it (or GL optimisation, #43) with confidence. CubicGrid's default 27,000-point grid ran at 5.6 to 6 fps, which he found too slow; 20 ticks runs at 11 to 12 fps and he likes the look better.

**How to apply:** use `uv run tools/gl_budget.py <name>` to price a GL hack before porting (reads unported hacks from `vendor/`), trust it to about 10 percent for ranking, and add each new port's measured step to the accuracy table. A new GL hack follows the Gears pattern: byte-identical copy, `hacks/<name>_gl.c` wrapper with `#define USE_GL`, exclude the directory in all three `build_src_filter` lines, `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH` in `registry.c`, a leak test using `start_step_and_stop_gl_hack`. Related: [[project-gears-gl-landed]], [[project-tinygl-pipes-spike]], [[project-board-and-open-work]].

---
name: project-board-and-open-work
description: "What is flashed on the StopWatch and which tickets are open, as of the end of the 2026-10-09/10 GL session (state git cannot show)"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
---

State at the end of the 2026-10-09/10 session. `main` has the badge, battery readout, Gears, Morph3D, CubicGrid and `tools/gl_budget.py`. The badge text is `-DBADGE_NAME` and defaults to "Rod". The "Rod B." build was only ever a temporary test: **Rod said to stop passing it, so use the default name from now on.**

**The board is running a temporary test build, not a plain `main`.** It was last flashed pinned to CubicGrid with `-DSTART_HACK` and `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`; an overnight rotating capture (`-DROTATE_SECONDS=10`, issue #50) was planned for about an hour after Rod's bedtime message, which will replace it. Either way the next flash that should happen is a plain build of `main`, which needs Rod's go-ahead. Maze shows no WorkOS icon unless `XS_LOGO` is set; my builds do not set it.

Open tickets (checked with `gh issue list`): #31 (harden XFillArc and canvas_fill_polygon against signed overflow), #32 (Pacman: random level design), #37 (Celtic: out of the rotation at 1.2 fps and 300 KB heap), #43 (TinyGL setup cost), #44 and #46 (GL ideas, missing TinyGL features), #50 (long rotating capture: Morph3D middle shapes and CubicGrid leaks). Closed this session: #41 (stale xlockmore flag) and #45 (GL candidate survey).

The badge adds about 16 to 20 ms to `push=`; Galaxy's delay slack hides it, Squiral drops from 88 to 46 fps. Push also read 36 ms instead of 32 ms in the first window of captures (the overlay stamp), so read `push=` from the second window.

**Why:** none of this is visible from git, and a temporary pinned or rotating build would surprise whoever next looks at the board.

**How to apply:** at the start of a session, ask whether the board should get a plain flash of `main`. Flashing needs Rod's go-ahead for each request, though an explicit request to run a capture that needs a flash (rotation on) has counted as covering that one flash. Related: [[stopwatch-device-gotchas]], [[project-gl-budget-and-gl-ports]], [[feedback-verify-pr-body-after-trail-create]], [[feedback-branch-cleanup-after-merge]].

input.project_notes: stopwatch-screensaver, GL session 2026-10-09/10. Shipped: gl_budget.py host harness (private instrumented TinyGL; counters at glopVertex and the draw_triangle_front/back call sites so display-list replays count each frame), Morph3D (#48) and CubicGrid (#49, *ticks 20) on the GL layer. Accuracy vs device about 10% on four scenes not in the fit. Decisions that held: count inside TinyGL not at the API (cubicgrid is one display list replayed every frame); fit only pixel_ns to the heavy Gears scene and hold out the light one; port both hacks unmodified behind a USE_GL wrapper. Surprises: (1) the plan's own tolerances (10%/20%) passed with pixel_ns halved, so the mutation check the plan asked for could not fail; tightening the tests (fill term pinned to 40 ms, light scene to 8%) fixed it. (2) Morph3D's one-element GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE array exposed a real TinyGL overrun in glLightModelfv (always copies four floats); only ASan on the host found it, the non-ASan dump build ran clean. (3) the fresh-context review caught that my doc claimed morph3d was robust to the fill model when its triangles are 3-4 px against Gears' 15-30, and that it has two lights; on the board neither mattered (within 4%), so the claim was wrong but the worry was too. Pending: issue #50 (Morph3D's two middle shapes never seen because the device does not seed random(); CubicGrid leak lap) and an overnight rotating capture.
input.technical_insights: A test tolerance that is looser than the effect of the mutation you are checking is a test that cannot fail: when a plan says 'mutation-check this' and the check passes with the key constant halved, treat that as a finding about the test, not a pass. Also: when an ASan-only failure appears in a test sequence, rerun the same hack in the non-ASan build before assuming it is flaky; the same code ran clean there. A cost model fitted to one scene can look validated by a second scene that happens to share its pixels-per-triangle ratio; the held-out check is only as independent as the scenes are different, so say that in the write-up.

input.content:
📐 Built a host-side "polygon budget" tool for a tiny round ESP32 display, then used it to pick and port two OpenGL screensavers. It predicted the on-device frame time to about 10%. 🎯

The lessons were the interesting bit:
🧪 My own plan's test tolerances passed with the key constant HALVED, so the mutation check couldn't fail. The tolerance was looser than the thing it guarded. Tighten until the mutation bites.
🐛 Porting Morph3D hit a real out-of-bounds read in TinyGL (glLightModelfv always copies 4 floats, even for a 1-float param). Only AddressSanitizer saw it; the non-ASan build ran clean.
🔍 A fresh-context reviewer caught that my write-up claimed a model was robust where it wasn't. On the real board the worry didn't bite, but the claim was still wrong. Check the claim, not just the outcome.
⏳ Still unseen: two of Morph3D's four random shapes, because the device never seeds random(). Tonight's job is a 2-hour rotating capture to wait for them. 🌙

#embedded #opengl #testing #espidf

content.text:
Yes. The three hacks change the picture quite a bit. This is analysis only, and I haven't touched any code or the device.

**Where a frame goes** (measured step and push, with the step split using the #43 constants):

| Hack | Step | Of which clear | Setup | Push | Frame |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CubicGrid, 8,000 points | 48–52 ms | about 25 | about 25–32 | 32 | about 82 ms |
| Morph3D, heavy shape | 78–82 ms | about 25 | about 49 | 33–36 | about 113 ms |
| Gears, light layout | about 65 ms | about 25 | about 29 | 34 | about 100 ms |

Clear and push are the fixed 56 ms floor. For the light scenes, which are the ones we ship, setup is under half of the step. The issue's ideas are mostly about setup, which matters least here.

**What I'd rank, biggest first:**

1. **Overlap the push with the next frame's render.** Today the loop is strictly serial: `runner_step`, then a blocking `present()`, then the wait. If the push ran on core 0 while core 1 rendered the next frame, a frame would cost `max(step, push)` instead of `step + push`. That would give roughly:
   - **CubicGrid:** 12 to about 20 fps.
   - **Morph3D heavy:** 8.8 to about 12.5 fps.
   - **Gears light:** 10 to about 15 fps.
   - **Gears heavy:** only about 10%, since it's render-bound.

   There is no visual change. It can be done in `glshim` for GL hacks only, at `glXSwapBuffers`, since GL hacks redraw everything each frame. 2D hacks accumulate on the canvas, so they can't be double-buffered. It needs a second 434 KB buffer in PSRAM, which we have room for. The risks:
   - **PSRAM bandwidth:** the push reads PSRAM while the renderer clears and writes it, and clear is already bandwidth-bound (868 KB in 24.6 ms). The real gain could be well under the ideal figure.
   - **M5GFX thread safety:** the main core also does overlay pushes and touch/battery I2C, so those need a lock.
   - **Scope:** it touches `main.cpp`'s present path, so it needs a design discussion.
2. **A one-line float fix.** `CLIP_EPSILON` is `(1E-5)`, a double literal, and it sits inside `gl_clipcode` (`w = w1 * (1.0f + CLIP_EPSILON)`). That's a software double multiply plus conversions on every vertex. Changing it to `1.00001f` in `tinygl_patch.py` is safe and testable. I'd estimate 2–6 ms on CubicGrid (about 8% of its step), but that's my guess, not a measurement. It's cheap, so it's the one to try first. The other `sqrt`/`pow` calls already map to the float versions.
3. **Skip the z-buffer clear when depth test is off.** CubicGrid never enables depth test, yet TinyGL clears 434 KB of z every frame, which is about 12 ms or a quarter of its step. It would need a lazy clear (clear on the first draw after depth test is enabled), or it would break a hack that clears and then enables depth test. It only helps point and line hacks, since Gears and Morph3D both use depth test.
4. **Profile before touching setup.** The repo's own technique (an early return in the hot function, as for Braid) would show where the 4–6.8 µs a vertex goes. CubicGrid is a good benchmark, since it's deterministic, with a fixed 8,000 unlit points. Gears' first layout after boot is also fixed, so it covers the lit path.
5. **Product choices that cost no engineering** (yours to make):
   - **Specular:** it's off today, so Gears has no highlights, and turning it on costs speed.
   - **Lighter Gears layouts:** a Galaxy-style `*count` override, which trades variety for speed.

**How I'd run this:**
- **Measurement:** use the pinned CubicGrid and Gears builds, read `step=` from the second 5-second window, and compare against the same build before the change.
- **Safety net:** the pinned frame hashes in `test_hacks` fail if any change alters the pixels, so I'd know a "free" speed-up isn't changing the picture.
- **Harness role:** it can confirm the counts are unchanged, but it can't measure device time per vertex. That part has to be measured on the board, as #43 says.

**Scheduling:** experiments need the board, and the overnight capture is coming. I'd do (2) as a design write-up now, run (1) on the board before bedtime if you're up, and leave the board alone for the capture after that.

Which would you like first? My pick is the one-line float fix as a quick win, then a design sketch for the overlap, since that's the big one.

content.text:
The one-line fix works: it takes **5.6 ms** off CubicGrid's step, which is about 11% of the step. It's committed on `feature/43-clip-epsilon-float` (686eac9), unpushed.

**The change.** `CLIP_EPSILON` was `1E-5`, which is a `double`. `gl_clipcode` multiplied every vertex's `w` by it, so each vertex ran a software double multiply and two conversions. It's now `1E-5f` in `tools/tinygl_patch.py`, with a test that failed before the patch. `src/tinygl/` is still byte-identical.

**Measurements on the board.**
- **CubicGrid (the clean A/B):** I flashed alternating baseline and patched builds, three boots of each. The boots are deterministic, so the three runs of each build agree to 0.1 ms. The patched build is faster by a flat 5.6 ms in every window (46.7 against 52.3 ms in the first window, 42.1 against 47.7 in the last). That works out to about 0.7 µs a vertex, at the top of my 2–6 ms guess.
- **Morph3D:** about 3 ms faster (77.8 against 81.1 ms mean over nine windows). That's less certain, because its morph cycle was out of phase between the two boots. Treat it as roughly 3 ms, not an exact figure.
- **One unexplained outlier:** an earlier baseline capture read 54.9 ms, against 52.3 ms on the three A/B boots. I can't explain it.

**Checks:**
- **Native tests:** all 312 pass, including the pinned frame hashes, so the pixels are unchanged.
- **Tools tests:** the patch tests pass.
- **Device:** the A/B above ran on the board.

**Notes updated.** `gl.md` now says what was fixed and that `gl_shade_vertex` hasn't been checked for `double` the same way. `docs/gl-budget.md` says the model's per-vertex cost is about 0.7 µs high on a build with this fix, until it's refitted. I didn't change the model's constants, because that would churn the Gears calibration tests, and I'd rather refit once after more optimisations.

**The 1 am capture:** it's rescheduled, and the old timer is stopped. If this branch isn't merged by then, I'll build the capture from plain `main`, so the shapes stay comparable to the published table. If you merge it first, I'll use that and note it in the results.

**The board** is on a patched Morph3D build, pinned with rotation off and the default badge.

**Next:** want me to open a draft PR for this, then look at `gl_shade_vertex` for the same kind of double-precision leak? That's the lit-path equivalent. It could help Morph3D and Gears more than CubicGrid, since they use lighting.

## Summary

The first optimisation from #43. Refs #43.

TinyGL's `CLIP_EPSILON` was `1E-5`, a `double`. `gl_clipcode` multiplies every
vertex's `w` by `1.0f + CLIP_EPSILON`, so each vertex ran a software `double`
multiply and two conversions on the ESP32-S3, which has a single-precision FPU
only. `tools/tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`. `src/tinygl/` stays
byte-identical, and the patch checks its anchor like the others.

## Measured on the board

A/B with alternating builds, three boots of each, CubicGrid pinned with
rotation off (8,000 unlit points a frame). Its boots are deterministic, so the
three runs of each build agree to 0.1 ms:

| Window | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | 52.3 ms | 46.7 ms |
| Last (ninth) | 47.7 ms | 42.1 ms |

A flat 5.6 ms off the step in every window (about 11 percent), or about
0.7 us a vertex. Morph3D, which runs the lit path, went from a mean step of
81.1 to 77.8 ms over nine windows (about 3 ms); that comparison is less clean,
because its morph cycle was out of phase between the two boots.

## Verified

- `pio test -e native`: 312 of 312, including the pinned frame hashes, so
  nothing renders differently. The tools tests pass, including a new one for
  this patch that failed first.
- On the device: the CubicGrid A/B above, and a Morph3D capture.

## Not verified

- Only CubicGrid and Morph3D were timed; Gears was not.
- One earlier CubicGrid baseline capture read 54.9 ms, against 52.3 ms on the
  three A/B boots. It is unexplained.
- The model constants in `docs/gl-budget.md` predate this change, so its vertex
  cost is about 0.7 us high on a build with it. Not refitted yet, to avoid
  churning the Gears calibration tests after each optimisation.

After the clip-epsilon fix (#43), CubicGrid's step at 8,000 points is 46.7 ms
in its first window. Temporary early returns in TinyGL, built only for the
experiment and never committed, split it on the board (each boot is
deterministic, so windows compare directly):

| Part | Time | Share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Colour clear (a build with no colour clear ran at 34.0 ms) | 12.7 ms | 27% |
| List read and op dispatch, the hack's own work (the rest of the 22.3 ms floor left when `glopVertex` returns at once) | about 9.6 ms | 21% |
| Vertex pipeline: transform, clip code, projection (35.6 ms with `gl_draw_point` also skipped, less the floor) | 13.3 ms, about 1.7 us a vertex | 28% |
| `gl_draw_point` | 11.1 ms, about 1.4 us a point | 24% |

What this says for #43:

- **`gl_shade_vertex` has no `double` work left on the per-vertex path** for
  these hacks. After the epsilon fix the only soft-double references in
  TinyGL are `glFrustum`, `glopLight`, `glopRotate`, `glClearDepth` and a debug
  printer (all per call), and two compares against `1E-3` in `gl_shade_vertex`
  that run only for positional lights and specular. Gears and Morph3D use
  directional lights with specular off, so they never run. That patch would be
  a guess without a hack to time it on.
- **CubicGrid asks only for a colour clear**, so skipping a z clear would save
  nothing there, and Gears and Morph3D need theirs for depth test.
- **The colour clear runs at about 34 MB/s** (434 KB in 12.7 ms), and the list
  is probably also read from PSRAM at about that rate, which is a guess, not a
  measurement. These costs are memory bandwidth, not arithmetic.
- **Untried, and the largest idea on the table:** a dirty-rectangle for GL.
  Track the bounding box of everything drawn, clear only that box and push only
  its rows. Morph3D's flower is about 70 px across and wanders over a 250 px
  range, so it might cut its clear from about 25 to 7 ms and its push from 33 to
  about 18 ms (about 9 to 13 fps by arithmetic, not measured). CubicGrid's
  points span the whole screen, so it would gain nothing. Overlapping the push
  with the next frame is the other big lever (see #43).

''' + a,1)
open(p,"w").write(s)
E

content.text:
PR #51 is open as a draft, and the `gl_shade_vertex` look found no per-vertex `double` work left to remove. It's still 23:46, so there are about 75 minutes before the 1 am capture.

**PR #51** is https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/pull/51 (trail 28). It holds the epsilon fix, with the A/B table in the body. I pushed one more commit to it with the profile findings below, and the first push was rejected before the retry went through.

**`gl_shade_vertex`:**
- **No per-vertex doubles left:** after the epsilon fix, TinyGL's only remaining soft-double references are per call (`glFrustum`, `glopLight`, `glopRotate`, `glClearDepth`, a debug printer), plus two `1E-3` compares in `gl_shade_vertex`.
- **Those compares never run for us:** they only run for positional lights and specular. Gears and Morph3D use directional lights with specular off.
- **No change made:** I left the two compares alone rather than ship a guess I can't time. I found this by reading the code and checking the object file for double-helper references.

**Where CubicGrid's 46.7 ms step goes.** I measured this with temporary early-returns in TinyGL, flashed repeatedly. The profiling edits were never committed and are gone from the tree and the binary.

| Part | Time | Share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Colour clear | 12.7 ms | 27% |
| Vertex pipeline | 13.3 ms | 28% |
| Drawing the points | 11.1 ms | 24% |
| List read and dispatch | about 9.6 ms | 21% |

The last row is derived from the rest of the floor, and the cause (reading the list from PSRAM) is my guess, not measured. The clear writes at about 34 MB/s, so these costs are memory bandwidth, not arithmetic.

**Two ideas I dropped:**
- **Skipping the z clear:** CubicGrid only clears colour, and Gears and Morph3D need their depth clear.
- **Lighting patch:** nothing to patch for these hacks.

**Biggest untried idea for #43: a dirty rectangle for GL.** Track the bounding box of what was drawn, then clear and push only that area:
- **Morph3D:** its flower is about 70 px across and wanders over about 250 px. By arithmetic, clear could fall from about 25 to 7 ms and push from 33 to about 18 ms, so roughly 9 to 13 fps. Nothing has been measured.
- **CubicGrid:** no gain, since its points span the whole screen.
- **Overlap:** overlapping the push with the next frame is still the other big lever.

**The board** is on a sane patched CubicGrid build, pinned with rotation off and the default badge. It isn't on any profiling build.

**For the 1 am capture:** PR #51 isn't merged, so I'll build from plain `main`, as planned. If you merge it first I'll use that and say so in the results.

**Next:** want me to prototype the dirty-rectangle idea on a branch, starting with a measurement-only version that counts how much of the canvas each hack really touches? That would tell us whether it's worth building before we write any clearing or push logic.

        "glVertex3f(dx,.2f,0); glEnd();"

def render_report(rows: list[dict]) -> str:
    lines = [
        "| Hack | Seed | Vertices | Lit | Triangles | Lines | Points | Pixels "
        "| Box % | Clear % | Push % | Predicted ms | Predicted fps | Note |",
        "| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |",
    ]
    for row in rows:
        note = note_for(row)
        if "counts" in row:
            c = row["counts"]
            numbers = (
                f"{c.vertices:.0f} | {c.lit_vertices:.0f} | {c.triangles:.0f} | "
                f"{c.lines:.0f} | {c.points:.0f} | {c.pixels:.0f}"
            )
            if c.vertices == 0:
                prediction = "- | -"
            else:
                ms = predict_ms(c)
                prediction = f"{ms:.0f} | {fps(ms):.1f}"
        else:
            numbers = " | ".join("-" for _ in COUNTER_NAMES)
            prediction = "- | -"
        lines.append(
            f"| {row['name']} | {row['seed']} | {numbers} | {prediction} | {note} |"
        )
    model = ", ".join(f"{key}={value:g}" for key, value in MODEL.items())
    return "\n".join(lines) + f"\n\nPredictions, not measurements. Model: {model}.\n"


def parse_arguments(argv: list[str]) -> argparse.Namespace:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Predict the device frame rate of GL hacks from host counts."
    )
    parser.add_argument("--frames", type=int, default=300)
    parser.add_argument(
        "--seeds",
        default=",".join(map(str, DEFAULT_SEEDS)),
        help="comma-separated seeds tried for each hack without its own",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "hacks", nargs="+", help="hack name, or name:seed to give it one seed"
    )
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    seeds = [int(seed) for seed in args.seeds.split(",")]
    parsed = []
    for spec in args.hacks:
        name, _, seed = spec.partition(":")
        parsed.append((name, [int(seed)] if seed else seeds))
    args.hacks = parsed
    return args

/* The GL context layer. TinyGL draws straight into the canvas, so a "swap"
 * only has to mark the canvas dirty. Not derived from xscreensaver code. */
#include "glshim/glshim.h"

#include <math.h>

#include "core/canvas.h"
#include "zbuffer.h"

static ZBuffer *g_zb;
static Canvas *g_canvas;

"""Patches that make TinyGL run on the StopWatch.

The copy in `firmware/src/tinygl/` stays byte-identical to upstream (the
C-Chads fork, commit 36a7987). The firmware build writes a patched tree into
the build directory with `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` and compiles that, as it
does for Maze and Pacman. Each patch checks what it replaces and fails loudly
if upstream has changed.

What the patches do, and why:

- 16-bit pixels, written byte-swapped: the canvas holds RGB565 with its bytes
  already swapped into display order, so TinyGL draws straight into it with no
  copy.
- A PSRAM-aware allocator: the z-buffer is 434 KB and the internal heap is
  325 KB.
- `glGenLists` starts at 1: hacks treat list name 0 as "invalid" and abort.
- `OP_BUFFER_MAX_SIZE` is 64, not 4096: every display list otherwise takes a
  16 KB buffer, and Pipes alone makes 500 of them.
- The buffer width is not rounded down to a multiple of 4: the canvas is 466.
- `memset_s` is renamed: macOS's `string.h` declares its own.
- Single precision: the S3's FPU does only `float`, so `double` maths is
  software. Decimal literals get an `f` suffix (`float_literals.py`) and
  `sqrt`, `pow`, `sin`, `cos` and `floor` map to their `f` versions.
"""

import hashlib
from collections.abc import Iterable, Mapping
from dataclasses import dataclass

import float_literals

p="docs/gl-budget.md"

  box a hack drew). It is prototyped below; overlapping the push with the next
  frame is the other big lever and is untried.

## Dirty rectangle prototype (#43)

`tools/gl_budget.py` now reports, per frame, the box around what a hack drew
and what clearing and pushing only that area would cost, as a percentage of the
canvas. Over 300 frames:

| Hack | Box | Clear | Push |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Morph3D, all four shapes | 6 to 9% | 6 to 9% | 7 to 9% |
| Gears, four seeds (light to heaviest) | 19 to 27% | 19 to 27% | 19 to 27% |
| CubicGrid | 100% | 100% | 100% |

Morph3D's flower is small, so the box is far smaller than the 30 percent I
first guessed. The prototype (`glshim_note_box` and `glshim_clear` in
`firmware/src/glshim/glshim.c`, hooked in by `tools/tinygl_patch.py`) tracks
that box. `glClear` clears only the box drawn since the last clear; a swap
marks only what was drawn and what the clear erased. A new context starts with
a full clear and a full push, and a new clear colour is a full clear, so it
cannot leave stale pixels behind. It assumes nothing else draws on the canvas
while a GL hack runs, which the overlay already respects (it restores what it
stamps).

On the board, same boots, step and push in ms (rows is the canvas rows sent a
frame, out of 466):

| Hack | Before | Dirty rectangle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Morph3D | step 75 to 83, push 32.5, wait 8.8, rows 466, 8.2 to 8.8 fps | step 55 to 59, push 2 to 9, wait 34 to 42, rows 92 to 192, 9.8 to 10.2 fps |
| Morph3D, `*delay: 10000` (temporary) | | step 57 to 58, push 2 to 9, wait 2.6 to 9.4, 14.4 to 14.8 fps |
| Gears, first layout after boot | step 65 to 79, push 32 to 34, wait 0, 9.0 to 10.2 fps | step 44 to 63, push 4 to 12, wait 20 to 29, rows 194 to 303, 10.6 to 13.0 fps |
| CubicGrid | step 46.7, push 32, rows 466 | step 47.7, push 32, rows 466 |

- **The work shrinks a lot and the frame rate barely follows**, because both
  hacks ask for a pause after each frame (`*delay` 40 ms for Morph3D, 30 ms for
  Gears) and the loop only credits the push against it. Morph3D's frame is now
  step plus a 40 ms pause. Shortening the pause is a per-hack registry override
  and a taste call; with 10 ms Morph3D reached 14.6 fps, 75 percent over the
  8.4 fps it started the evening at.
- **CubicGrid pays about 1 ms (2 percent)** for the bookkeeping on every point,
  and gains nothing, because its points span the whole screen.
- **Correctness:** the pinned frame hash of every hack is unchanged, so the
  output is pixel-identical, and the shadow-display replay in `test_push_present`
  still passes, so no changed row went unmarked. New tests in `test_glshim`
  cover a moving box, depth, a new clear colour and the first frame.
- The cost model's clear and push constants (24.6 and 32 ms) assume a full
  canvas; with this change they scale by the percentages above.

''' + s[j:]
open(p,"w").write(s)
E

## Summary

A prototype of the biggest idea from the #43 profile. Refs #43. It is a
prototype: Rod asked for one, and this PR is for him to look at, not a request
to merge as it stands.

TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws (hooks added by
`tools/tinygl_patch.py` at the same points the harness uses). In
`firmware/src/glshim/glshim.c`, `glClear` clears only the box drawn since the
last clear, and `glXSwapBuffers` marks only what was drawn and what the clear
erased, so the display push sends those rows instead of all 466. A new context
starts with a full clear and a full push, and a new clear colour is a full
clear. It assumes nothing else draws on the canvas while a GL hack runs.

`tools/gl_budget.py` also reports how much of the canvas a hack touches, which
is what said this was worth building: Morph3D 6 to 9 percent, Gears 19 to 27,
CubicGrid 100.

## Measured on the board

| Hack | Before | Dirty rectangle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Morph3D | step 75 to 83 ms, push 32.5, 8.2 to 8.8 fps | step 55 to 59, push 2 to 9, 9.8 to 10.2 fps |
| Morph3D, `*delay: 10000` (temporary, not in this PR) | | 14.4 to 14.8 fps |
| Gears, first layout | step 65 to 79, push 32 to 34, 9.0 to 10.2 fps | step 44 to 63, push 4 to 12, 10.6 to 13.0 fps |
| CubicGrid | step 46.7, push 32 | step 47.7, push 32 |

The work shrinks a lot, but both hacks ask for a pause after each frame (40 ms
for Morph3D, 30 ms for Gears) and the loop only credits the push against it, so
the frame rate barely follows. Shortening that pause is a per-hack registry
override and Rod's call. CubicGrid pays about 1 ms (2 percent) for bookkeeping
and cannot gain, as its points cover the whole screen.

## Verified

- `pio test -e native`: 318 of 318. Every hack's pinned frame hash is unchanged,
  so output is pixel-identical, and the shadow-display replay in
  `test_push_present` passes, so no changed row went unmarked. Six new
  `test_glshim` tests (a moving box, depth, a new clear colour, the first
  clear, the swap's rows, and that only the drawn region is rewritten); the
  last two failed first. Tools tests: 91.
- On the device: the measurements above.

## Not verified

- **Nobody has looked at the screen with this on.** Stale pixels would show as
  trails or ghosts around the moving flower or the gears; the host checks
  cannot see what the display itself does with partial pushes.
- Only Morph3D, Gears and CubicGrid were run, with one boot each for Gears and
  CubicGrid; Morph3D's shape is random per boot.
- A long run for leaks or drift has not been done on this build; it adds no
  allocation (a few static boxes), and the host leak tests pass.
- It has not been merged with the delay question: the registered delays are
  unchanged.

content.text:
Rod, the dirty-rectangle prototype is built, measured and open as draft PR #52. **It's on the board for you to look at.** I haven't seen the screen, and stale pixels are the thing the tests can't see.

**What it does.** TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws. `glClear` clears only the box drawn since the last clear, and the swap marks only the old and new boxes, so the push sends just those rows. A new context starts with a full clear and push, and a new clear colour is a full clear. It assumes nothing else draws on the canvas while a GL hack runs.

**What the host harness said first** (percent of canvas): Morph3D uses 6–9%, Gears 19–27% and CubicGrid 100%. That's what told me it was worth building.

**On the board** (same boots):

| Hack | Before | Dirty rectangle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Morph3D | step 75–83 ms, push 32.5, 8.2–8.8 fps | step 55–59, push 2–9, 9.8–10.2 fps |
| Morph3D, with a 10 ms delay | | **14.4–14.8 fps** |
| Gears, first layout | step 65–79, push 32–34, 9.0–10.2 fps | step 44–63, push 4–12, 10.6–13.0 fps |
| CubicGrid | step 46.7 ms | 47.7 ms (about 2% slower, no gain) |

**The surprise: the work shrank a lot, but the frame rate barely moved.** Morph3D asks for a 40 ms pause after each frame, and Gears 30 ms, and the loop only credits the push against it. So most of the saving turns into waiting. Shortening Morph3D's pause to 10 ms is what gets it to 14.6 fps, 75% above where it started tonight. That override is a taste call, so it's yours, and it isn't in the PR.

**Correctness:**
- **Frame hashes:** all 318 native tests pass, and every hack's pinned frame hash is unchanged, so the output is pixel-identical.
- **Shadow display:** the replay still passes, so no changed row went unmarked.
- **New tests:** six, two of which failed first.

**What I'd like you to look at.** The board is on Morph3D pinned with the dirty rectangle and the temporary 10 ms delay, rotation off. Look for trails, ghosts or leftover bits around the wandering flower. I can also flash Gears or CubicGrid if you'd like to check those.

**The 1 am capture is still on.** It builds from plain `main`, which now includes the epsilon fix but not this prototype, so the Morph3D shapes and CubicGrid leak data stay comparable to what's published. I'll write it up on its own branch in the morning.

**Decisions for you:**
- **Per-hack delays:** shorten them for Morph3D and Gears, or leave the hacks' own pacing?
- **Merge:** whether this prototype should go to `main` as is, once you've looked at the screen.
- **Overlap push:** whether to try overlapping the push with the next frame, the other big idea.

**The pause change.**

- **Test:** it has its own test, which failed before the change.
- **Gears:** it keeps its 30 ms pause.

**On the board with the registered build** (the committed version, matching the earlier experiment window for window):
- **Rate and step:** Morph3D ran at 14.4–15.2 fps, with a step of 54–58 ms.
- **Push:** 2–9 ms, sending 91–162 of the 466 rows.
- **Stability:** no resets or panics.
- **Since this evening:** that's about 75% above the 8.4 fps it started the evening at.

**Checks:** the native suite passes 319 of 319, including every hack's pinned frame hash, so output is unchanged. The tools tests pass (91).

**What's in the PR:**
- **Dirty rectangle:** the prototype that clears and pushes only the touched box.
- **Coverage report:** the `gl_budget` coverage report.

466×466 round AMOLED) through a small X11 shim. A learning project: explain
embedded-specific choices as you make them. See `README.md` for setup and
`docs/porting-assessment.md` for what to port next.

## Layout

- `firmware/src/hacks/<name>/`: hack sources copied from xscreensaver.
  `hacks/registry.[ch]` (ours) lists them in button order.
- `firmware/src/glshim/` (ours) is the GL layer for OpenGL hacks, over
  `firmware/src/tinygl/` (TinyGL, byte-identical, patched at build by
  `tools/tinygl_patch.py`). `xs_support/glx/` holds the copied GL helpers.
  Gears is the first GL hack.
- `tools/failed_ports.txt` lists abandoned ports (`name: reason`); the scorer
  marks them ❌, and ✅ comes from `g_hacks[]` in `registry.c`.
- `.claude/skills/port-hack/`: the order of work for porting a hack, and a
  recipe per trap (`techniques.md`). Use it when porting or fixing a ported
  hack. `m5stack-stopwatch/` is the board guide.
- `.agents/skills/`: symlinks to `.claude/skills/` so non-Claude agents find
  the skills. Leave it alone.
- `vendor/`, `backups/`, `.venv/`, `.platformio/` are git-ignored and local.

## Commands

Run `source tools/env.sh` first (keeps PlatformIO inside the repo), then from
`firmware/`:

- `pio test -e native`: host tests (Unity, AddressSanitizer). Run these first.
- `pio run -e stopwatch`: build for the device. Add `-t upload` to flash.
  The device starts on a random hack; to pin one while examining it, prefix
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS='-DSTART_HACK=\"galaxy\"'` (a name from `g_hacks[]`,
  any case; an unknown name falls back to random and logs it). Rebuild without
  it afterwards, since the define sticks to the build.
  It rotates to the next hack every 90 s (a button press restarts the count);
  `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5` shortens that for leak testing and `=0` turns it off. A
  pinned build still rotates, so add `=0` to measure one hack.
  The log prints `rotate -> <hack> heap= psram=` at each change. Combine flags
  in one `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` string.
  `-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod\ B.\"` sets the name badge text (default "Rod"). Check a
  flag reached the binary with
  `strings -a -n 3 .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c '^Rod B\.$'`:
  plain `strings` skips anything under 4 characters.
  In a worktree session the harness refuses backslash-escaped flag values and
  `$(cat file)`. Use `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="'-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod B.\"'
  '-DSTART_HACK=\"gears\"' -DROTATE_SECONDS=0"` with `.venv/bin/pio run -d
  firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` from the worktree root.
- `pio run -e dump`, then `.pio/build/dump/program <index> <frames> out.raw`,
  then `uv run tools/rgb565_to_png.py out.raw 466 466 out.png` to see a frame.
  The index is the hack's 0-based position in `g_hacks[]` in
  `hacks/registry.c` (Hopalong is 13, Galaxy 21, Drift 22, Maze 24, Blaster
  25, Substrate 26): look it up, and check the dumped hack by name before
  trusting a comparison. With 0 frames it starts and stops the hack, which
  shows at once whether one survives being freed before its first draw (an
  exit code of 139 is a crash). `pio test` and `pio run -e stopwatch` delete
  `.pio/build/dump/program`: rebuild `-e dump` before `dump stats` or
  `tools/speed_backtest.py`.
- To compare frames side by side, write a small `uv run` script with an inline
  `pillow` dependency; the system Python has no PIL.
- Serial log: read `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` at 115200 for N seconds into a file
  (a pyserial script run with `.venv/bin/python -I`). Run it in the background
  with absolute paths, since background shells ignore `cd`. Lines to read:
  `run <hack> fps= step= push= wait= rows=` (ms per frame in the hack, the
  push and the wait; mean canvas rows sent per frame, 466 being a full push,
  though overlay redraws made while waiting can push it higher)
  and `switch -> <hack> press_waited=`. An empty capture, or "Device not
  configured", means the USB port went away and came back (a flash, a crash):
  reopen it in a loop. Opening the port resets the board
  (`rst:0x15 USB_UART_CHIP_RESET`, even with DTR/RTS held low): the overlay
  returns to nothing and a random hack starts. To measure one hack, flash a
  pinned build (`START_HACK` plus `ROTATE_SECONDS=0`), start the capture, then
  tap during it: the early windows are the baseline, the later ones have the
  overlay.
- Flash with `pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > file 2>&1`, never piped through
  `head`, and check for "Hash of data verified". The button steps backwards
  (Pyro, then Lightning, then Drift...). Work out how long a restart takes
  from the hack's cycle count times its frame time (Substrate: 10,000 cycles
  at about 160 ms is 27 minutes) and capture that long, with rotation off.
- `cc -O1 -fstack-usage -c src/hacks/<n>/<n>.c` (with `-Isrc
  -Isrc/x11shim/include -Isrc/xs_support -DXSHIM_NATIVE -DSTANDALONE`) lists
  stack frames; keep each well under the 16 KB loop stack.

From the repo root:

- `uv run --with pytest --with pillow pytest tools/tests` (without Pillow the
  logo converter's tests are skipped, not run)
- `uv run tools/check_notices.py`
- `uv run tools/score_hacks.py` regenerates `docs/porting-assessment.md`. It
  also builds each unported S hack with the shim and runs it on the host for the
  Speed column (`tools/probe_hacks.py`, about a minute); `--no-probe` skips it.
- `(cd firmware && pio run -e dump) && uv run tools/speed_backtest.py`
  regenerates `docs/speed-backtest.md`: host time against the step measured on
  the device, for every registered hack.
- `uv run tools/gl_budget.py cubicgrid morph3d` predicts a GL hack's device
  frame rate from vertex and fill counts taken on the host (`docs/gl-budget.md`
  has the model and its limits). It reads unported hacks from `vendor/`.
- `markdownlint <files>` (config in `.markdownlint.json`). Run it from here:
  from `firmware/` it misses the config and reports line-length errors.

Set `NO_COLOR=1` on `pio` output you parse.

## Rules

- **Copied hacks stay byte-identical** to `vendor/xscreensaver-*/hacks/`. Make
  them compile by extending the shim, never by editing the hack. Verify with
  `cmp`.
- **Licensing:** every copied file keeps its original header and gets a row
  in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`; `tools/check_notices.py` must pass. Read an
  unfamiliar file's licence before copying it (seven xscreensaver hacks do
  not use the standard jwz notice). Our own code is MIT.
- **Shim code is ours.** Do not copy xscreensaver's `utils/` files; write
  small equivalents in `x11shim/`.
- **Test first**, on the host. Clip arithmetic must use `int64_t`: the ESP32's
  `long` is 32 bits, so host tests cannot see 32-bit overflow.
- Mutation-check new tests: break the rule under test and watch the test fail.
  Race fixes need a failing two-thread stress test first (see `test_buttons`).
  A test can pass for the wrong reason: through Pyro, "starts black" passed
  with the runner broken (Pyro clears its own window), and "20 non-black
  pixels" passed on Substrate's white canvas before it drew. Test shared
  behaviour with stub hacks, and compare with the canvas the hack started on.
  Counting distinct colours could not see a consistent byte swap (a swap maps
  colours one to one): pin a hash of the frame instead, taken from a build you
  trust, and call `srandom(1)` first, because `random()` carries over between
  tests.
- Changing what every hack sees (the runner, a default, a shared helper) is not
  filling a shim gap: ask Rod first.
- Verify a delegated port yourself: `cmp` the hack, run the full suite, build
  for the device. Agents' reports have been wrong (a test count; "orange looks
  orange in a host frame" taken as proof of byte order).
- **Never flash, erase or write the device without asking Rod.** The
  conference firmware was backed up to `backups/` (git-ignored, one copy).
  Keep the `app3M_fat9M_16MB` partition scheme and never touch `ffat`. Serial
  port is `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401`; leave `/dev/cu.usbmodem14201` alone.
- Report "compiles", "host tests pass" and "runs on the device" separately.
  Only Rod can confirm what the screen shows: say when you want him to look,
  which hack, and what to check (colours on a picture whose colours you know).
- Python: 3.13+, `uv`, ruff, pytest. Markdown: invoke the `/markdown` skill.
- Commits end with the `Co-Authored-By` trailer from the session reminder.
  Use named paths with `git add`, never `-A`.

## Adding a hack

Use the `port-hack` skill. Its `adding-a-hack.md` holds the numbered steps.

## Delivering a branch

Use the `deliver-branch` skill.

## Gotchas

Gotchas tied to one area live in `.claude/rules/` and load when Claude reads
files there: `device-display.md` (main.cpp, core, runner), `x11shim.md`,
`hacks.md`, `gl.md` (glshim, tinygl, the GL helpers) and `tools-scoring.md`.
Add a new gotcha to the matching file. The
ones below apply everywhere.

- In `platformio.ini` use `platform = platformio/native`; plain `native`
  breaks `pio run`. Native tests need `test_build_src = yes`.
- Quoted includes resolve beside the including file first, so compile hack
  copies from a temp dir when checking them against the shim.
- Host tests cannot prove the 16 KB loop stack: `ulimit -s` sees only the
  shallow first level of a random recursion, and AddressSanitizer inflates
  frames. Use `stack_used_by` in `test_hacks.c` (a painted pthread stack) and,
  on the device, `uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark` in the stats line (temporary).
- `pio test` runs every registered hack for 3000 frames under ASan (about 15 s);
  a hack that is slow on the host slows the whole suite.
- Host leak tests: LeakSanitizer does not run on macOS, so compare
  `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`
  (`<sanitizer/allocator_interface.h>`) before and after many restarts, as in
  `test_hacks.c`.
- `pio test` hides `printf` and stderr from tests. To see two values, assert
  `TEST_ASSERT_EQUAL_UINT64(a, b)` temporarily: the failure line prints both.
- In a git worktree the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/` are
  missing. Symlink them from the main checkout. `.gitignore`'s trailing slashes
  don't match symlinks, so they would show as untracked, but the shared
  `.git/info/exclude` already lists the three names. That file is shared by
  every worktree: ask Rod before adding to it.
  The harness refuses `source tools/env.sh` and a computed `PATH` there: run
  `PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio ...` instead,
  and keep commands plain (no scripts, loops, `$VAR` in a command or `&&`
  chains with a computed path). A worktree an agent works in (`isolation:
  "worktree"`) starts from `origin/main`, not from your branch, and has no
  vendor or toolchain until you link them.
  It also refuses heredocs, `git -C` and `cd` into another worktree: use the
  Edit and Write tools. Parallel calls can race (a `uv run` in the root
  disturbed `.venv` while `pio` ran: "../.venv/bin/pio: no such file"), so run
  `uv` and `pio` one at a time. To fast-forward `main` or remove the worktree,
  leave it first with `ExitWorktree keep`.
  Before `ExitWorktree remove` on a merged branch, check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main`; the tool's "discarded N
  commits" count ignores merges. `.platformio`, `.venv` and `vendor` there are
  symlinks, so removal leaves the real ones alone.
- zsh does not word-split `$var`: loop over file lists with `bash -c`. It also
  stops on a glob that matches nothing, so quote `--include='*.c'`, and
  `grep` needs `-e` for a pattern that starts with a dash (`-e '->px'`).
- jwz.org returns 403 to Python's default User-Agent.
- `esptool` reads of the 16 MB flash need `--baud 921600` (about 3.5 minutes)
  and show no progress when piped.
- A push to GitHub is sometimes rejected once and succeeds on an immediate
  retry; never force-push for this.
- Read `push=` from a hack's second 5 s window on: the name overlay is stamped
  inside the push timing while it shows, so the first window reads high.
- Leak-testing with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5`: internal heap falls about 26 KB
  during the first lap and then stays flat. Compare lap 2 with lap 3, not
  with lap 1. PSRAM should match exactly on every visit.
- Mutation-checking wrap-around code: a mutation that just reorders unsigned
  arithmetic can be equivalent and survive. Use `int64_t` to break it for real.
- After a mutation check, `grep` that the change applied: a `sed` that matches
  nothing leaves the tests green and proves nothing. Restore the file and
  confirm with `cmp` or `git diff`.
- Board details (pins, power, recovery) are in
  `.claude/skills/m5stack-stopwatch/`.

- [Flash backup location](stopwatch-device-gotchas.md) — original firmware backup file and md5; other gotchas now live in AGENTS.md and .claude/rules/
- [Delete merged branches](feedback-branch-cleanup-after-merge.md) — after a PR merges, delete its branch without asking
- [Single-precision builds](single-precision-build-for-double-heavy-hacks.md) — float wrapper for double-heavy hacks (Galaxy 5→14 fps, Substrate 6→12.5); count the hot loop first
- [Merge without waiting for the gate](feedback-merge-without-waiting-for-gate.md) — Rod's approval is enough; merge, then clean up
- [Ask before force-with-lease](feedback-force-push-ask-each-time.md) — ask Rod each time after a rebase; he has approved each so far
- [AGENTS.md straight to main](feedback-agents-md-straight-to-main.md) — revisions go straight to main with no PR; he optimises it later
- [LinkedIn point of view](feedback-linkedin-pov.md) — "I" is Rod only, no "we"; name the agents as Claude
- [Board state and open work](project-board-and-open-work.md) — board runs a temporary test build (default badge name now); open: #31, #32, #37, #43, #44, #46, #50 (as of 2026-10-10)
- [Verify PR body after trail create](feedback-verify-pr-body-after-trail-create.md) — trail body doesn't reach the PR; read it back so Fixes #N works
- [Pacman and shim merged](project-pacman-port-state.md) — #30 and #33 on main 2026-10-09, board flashed with them, AGENTS.md updated; open issues #31 #32
- [Braid, Speed column, test ports](project-braid-and-scorer-speed.md) — #34, #35, #36 all merged 2026-10-09; Celtic shelved in open issue #37; next port from low-band S hacks
- [TinyGL / Pipes spike](project-tinygl-pipes-spike.md) — zlib licence, Pipes redraws the whole scene each frame, throwaway worktree spike-tinygl, shell-in-vendor gotcha
- [Gears landed](project-gears-gl-landed.md) — PR #47 merged 2026-10-09; speed follow-up #43, GL ideas #44-#46
- [GL budget tool and GL ports](project-gl-budget-and-gl-ports.md) — gl_budget.py, Morph3D and CubicGrid merged, about 10% accurate; #50 and an overnight capture pending

## Rules

- **Copied hacks stay byte-identical** to `vendor/xscreensaver-*/hacks/`. Make
  them compile by extending the shim, never by editing the hack. Verify with
  `cmp`.
- **Licensing:** every copied file keeps its original header and gets a row
  in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`; `tools/check_notices.py` must pass. Read an
  unfamiliar file's licence before copying it (seven xscreensaver hacks do
  not use the standard jwz notice). Our own code is MIT.
- **Shim code is ours.** Do not copy xscreensaver's `utils/` files; write
  small equivalents in `x11shim/`.
- **Test first**, on the host. Clip arithmetic must use `int64_t`: the ESP32's
  `long` is 32 bits, so host tests cannot see 32-bit overflow.
- Mutation-check new tests: break the rule under test and watch the test fail.
  Race fixes need a failing two-thread stress test first (see `test_buttons`).
  A test can pass for the wrong reason: through Pyro, "starts black" passed
  with the runner broken (Pyro clears its own window), and "20 non-black
  pixels" passed on Substrate's white canvas before it drew. Test shared
  behaviour with stub hacks, and compare with the canvas the hack started on.
  Counting distinct colours could not see a consistent byte swap (a swap maps
  colours one to one): pin a hash of the frame instead, taken from a build you
  trust, and call `srandom(1)` first, because `random()` carries over between
  tests.
- Changing what every hack sees (the runner, a default, a shared helper) is not
  filling a shim gap: ask Rod first.
- Verify a delegated port yourself: `cmp` the hack, run the full suite, build
  for the device. Agents' reports have been wrong (a test count; "orange looks
  orange in a host frame" taken as proof of byte order).
- **Never flash, erase or write the device without asking Rod.** The
  conference firmware was backed up to `backups/` (git-ignored, one copy).
  Keep the `app3M_fat9M_16MB` partition scheme and never touch `ffat`. Serial
  port is `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401`; leave `/dev/cu.usbmodem14201` alone.
- Report "compiles", "host tests pass" and "runs on the device" separately.
  Only Rod can confirm what the screen shows: say when you want him to look,

  missing. Symlink them from the main checkout. `.gitignore`'s trailing slashes
  don't match symlinks, so they would show as untracked, but the shared

  every worktree: ask Rod before adding to it.

  "worktree"`) starts from `origin/main`, not from your branch, and has no
  vendor or toolchain until you link them.
  It also refuses heredocs, `git -C` and `cd` into another worktree: use the
  Edit and Write tools. Parallel calls can race (a `uv run` in the root
  disturbed `.venv` while `pio` ran: "../.venv/bin/pio: no such file"), so run

  stops on a glob that matches nothing, so quote `--include='*.c'`, and

| Build | Step | Push | Wait | fps |

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

### 01M4JB21Q7162CA9ZKY9NVGNHP medium firmware/src/glshim/glshim.c 77
Dinesh vs Gilfoyle review (agent-run). fill_pixels stores through a uint32_t * into uint16_t memory: strict-aliasing UB. The ESP32 build uses -Os, which keeps strict aliasing on, and platformio.ini sets no -fno-strict-aliasing. Works today. Fix: memcpy the pair, or a may_alias typedef.

### 01M4JB20FR9QQ435F9TT8BJW6V high tools/tinygl_patch.py 91
Dinesh vs Gilfoyle review (agent-run, Claude under Rod's direction). DIRTY_LINE builds the box from p1 and p2 without ordering the endpoints, and glshim_note_box does not normalise them. When p1.x > p2.x (or y) the box is inverted, box_add treats it as empty, and the line is silently left out, leaving stale pixels. Latent: no default GL hack draws lines this way. Fix: min/max on both axes, plus a right-to-left line test.

### 01M4JB1RP4BMWR9MFR5R6Z24JS medium firmware/test/test_glshim/test_glshim.c None
Dinesh vs Gilfoyle review (agent-run). test_the_swap_marks_only_the_old_and_new_boxes_dirty passes with g_swap_erased deleted, because it never asserts that a row inside the first triangle's box is dirty. Add that assertion, then mutation-check. Related minor: test_a_region_clear_still_leaves_the_whole_canvas_clear draws one primitive per frame, so it cannot catch a box that fails to accumulate; add a second disjoint primitive.

### 01M4JB1PB4AA3HBCDK0VEJ23K2 medium tools/gl_budget.py None
Dinesh vs Gilfoyle review (agent-run). The budget tool re-implements the box with different rules from glshim_note_box: point margin 3 vs pointsize+1, line margin 0 vs 1, no empty-after-clamp check, so offscreen primitives inflate the box to the canvas edge. Reported Box/Clear/Push % is not what the firmware does. Share one rule or document the difference; add an offscreen-primitive test.

Entire Address Findings:

All five findings on trail 29 are fixed and resolved on the trail, and none are left open. The changes are uncommitted in the working tree on `feature/43-dirty-rect-spike`, ready for you to review, as the skill asks. The trail's branch matched the current one.

**Fixed:**

1. **High: right-to-left lines left stale pixels.** This was a real bug, and the review's description was right in spirit. The hook added its 1 px margin before ordering the endpoints, so a line drawn right-to-left produced a box two pixels too narrow. The hook now takes the min and max of each axis first. A new test that draws lines in all four directions failed first, and I added a patch-level test too.
2. **Medium: weak tests.**
   - **Swap test:** it now asserts a row in each triangle's band is dirty.
   - **Clear test:** it draws two disjoint primitives per frame.
   - **Mutation checks:** I removed the erased-box marking and made the box stop accumulating, and each change was caught by the matching test. Both are restored.
3. **Medium: the budget tool had its own box rules.** `glshim` now calls an observer hook that is NULL in the firmware, and the harness records the boxes it receives. So the harness measures exactly what the firmware does, and four new tests cover point size, an off-screen triangle, line direction and a clipped line. The point-size test failed first.

git branch --show-current && git status --short | head -2; tail -12 .claude/rules/gl.md | cut -c1-120; python3 - <<'E'
p=".claude/rules/gl.md"
s=open(p).read().rstrip("\n")
s+='''
- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding
  the margin: `p1.x - 1` to `p2.x + 1` shrinks a right-to-left line's box.
  `tools/gl_budget.py` gets its boxes from `glshim_box_observer` so it cannot
  drift from the firmware's rule.
- `glDrawPixels` keeps its data pointer in a 4-byte `GLParam`, so it cannot draw
  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.
  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same
  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed
  8,000 unlit points) and Gears' first layout after boot are the repeatable
  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a
  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.
- Overlapping the push with the next frame (core 0 pushing while core 1
  renders) is untried; it needs a second 434 KB buffer, a lock around M5GFX, and
  the PSRAM bandwidth may limit the gain.
'''
open(p,"w").write(s+"\n")
E

---
name: project-gl-budget-and-gl-ports
description: "GL hacks (Gears, Morph3D, CubicGrid), the gl_budget.py harness and the #43 speed work all merged by 2026-10-10: epsilon fix PR #51, dirty rectangle plus 10 ms pauses PR #52; #50 capture and the push-overlap idea still open"

  type: project

On `main` (as of 4ddb0a5, 2026-10-10): `tools/gl_budget.py` (host harness: counts, predicts frame time, reports canvas coverage, takes its boxes from `glshim_box_observer`), Morph3D (#48), CubicGrid at `*ticks: 20` (#49), the clip-epsilon fix (#51, `CLIP_EPSILON` was a double: 5.6 ms off CubicGrid's 52 ms step) and a dirty rectangle for GL clear and push (#52, with `*delay: 10000` for Morph3D and Gears and the five review findings fixed). Closed: #41, #45. Open: #43 (speed), #44, #46, #50.

Numbers on the board: Morph3D 8.4 fps at the start, 14.4 to 15.2 now; Gears' first layout 9 to 10 fps, now 12.6 to 17.6; CubicGrid unchanged (its points cover the whole canvas; it pays about 1 ms). The harness predicted frame times to about 10 percent (table in `docs/gl-budget.md`), but its clear and push constants (24.6 and 32 ms) assume a full canvas and now overstate Morph3D and Gears; refit before trusting it again. A CubicGrid frame splits as colour clear 27%, vertex pipeline 28%, drawing points 24%, list read and dispatch about 21%.

**Open work, in my order of value:** (1) #50: a long rotating capture (`-DROTATE_SECONDS=10`, two hours or more) for Morph3D's two middle shapes (5,040 and 5,100 vertices, never seen on the board) and CubicGrid leaks across restarts. It was scheduled for 1 am on 2026-10-10 from a background timer in the session that planned it, so check whether it ran before repeating it. (2) Overlap the push with the next frame (core 0 pushes, core 1 renders): untried, needs a second 434 KB buffer, a lock around M5GFX, and PSRAM bandwidth may limit it. (3) `gl_shade_vertex` has no per-vertex double left for these hacks (directional lights, specular off); do not patch its `1E-3` compares without a positional-light hack to time. (4) Refit `pixel_ns` and the clear/push constants in the harness.

**Why:** Rod wants GL speed work measured on the board before more ports, and the harness trusted only as far as it has been checked.

**How to apply:** use `uv run tools/gl_budget.py <name>` to price a hack before porting; a new GL hack follows the Gears pattern (byte-identical copy, `hacks/<name>_gl.c` wrapper with `#define USE_GL`, exclude the directory in all three `build_src_filter` lines, `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH`, a leak test using `start_step_and_stop_gl_hack`) and gets an accuracy row. Check a hack's own `*delay` before judging a speed-up: it hid most of the dirty rectangle's gain until it was cut. Gotchas are in `.claude/rules/gl.md`. Related: [[project-gears-gl-landed]], [[project-tinygl-pipes-spike]], [[project-board-and-open-work]].

input.project_notes: stopwatch-screensaver, second half of the 2026-10-09/10 GL session. Shipped: epsilon fix (#51), then a dirty rectangle for GL clear and push plus 10 ms pauses for Morph3D and Gears (#52), with five review findings fixed. Method that worked: the harness's coverage report said Morph3D touches 6-9% of the canvas before any firmware was written, so the prototype was justified by a host number. Alternating baseline and patched builds on the board, boot by boot, gave exact A/B (boots are deterministic; three boots agreed to 0.1 ms). Profiling by temporary early returns split a CubicGrid frame into clear 27%, vertex pipeline 28%, points 24%, list read 21%. Surprises: (1) the dirty rectangle cut Morph3D's step 78 to 57 ms and push 32 to 2-9 ms but fps barely moved, because the hack's own *delay (40 ms, only the push is credited against it) became the limit; cutting it to 10 ms is what delivered 8.4 to 14.6 fps. (2) The skip-z-clear idea I proposed was moot: CubicGrid only clears colour. (3) The review's high finding was real but its stated fix (order the endpoints) did not fix it; the margin was added before ordering, so the test stayed red until the min/max moved into the hook. (4) glDrawPixels cannot run on a 64-bit host (pointer in a 4-byte GLParam), so one finding got a patch-level test only. (5) My own plan's loose test tolerances earlier had hidden a mutation; tightening was the lesson that carried into this half (every finding got a mutation check). Pending: #50 capture (scheduled for 1 am from a background timer), push-overlap idea, harness refit.
input.technical_insights: When a speed-up shrinks the work but the frame rate barely moves, look for a fixed pause or rate cap in the loop before doubting the optimisation: here a per-hack *delay that credited only the push against it turned the saved time into waiting. Reproduce a review finding with a failing test before applying the reviewer's suggested fix; the suggested fix can be incomplete (ordering a box did not help when the margin was applied before the ordering). For embedded A/B timing, check first whether boots are deterministic; if they are, interleave builds and compare window by window, which is far tighter than comparing means across boots. A host harness can share a rule with the firmware by observing the firmware's own function through a NULL-in-production hook, instead of re-implementing it (the re-implementation had drifted: different margins, no empty check).

input.content:
🖼️ Taught a tiny ESP32 display to only redraw the part of the screen that changed, for software OpenGL screensavers. Morph3D went from 8.4 to 14.6 fps and Gears from ~9.6 to ~14.5. 🚀

What I learned on the way:
⏸️ The work per frame shrank a lot (step 78 to 57 ms, push 32 to 2-9 ms) but the frame rate barely moved. The hack's own "pause after each frame" setting was now the bottleneck, and the loop only credited the display push against it. Cutting the pause is what delivered the speed. Look for a rate cap before doubting the optimisation.
🔬 A reviewer's high-severity finding was REAL, but its suggested fix wasn't enough. Ordering a box's corners didn't help because the margin was added first. The failing test stayed red until the real cause moved. Reproduce first, then fix.
🔁 Boots on the board are deterministic, so I could alternate builds and compare window by window: three boots agreeing to 0.1 ms. Way tighter than comparing averages.
🪞 My host-side measurement tool had quietly re-implemented the firmware's box rule with different margins. Fix: observe the firmware's own function through a NULL-in-production hook, not a copy.
🌙 Overnight job still queued: a 2 hour capture to catch the two shapes of Morph3D I've never seen on the board.

#embedded #opengl #performance #testing
